Worker emergence is related to queen reproduction and survival in bumble-bee nests; animal life-history outcome is outside IWE plant-fitness scope.

Individual flowering phenology is related to interaction context and seed set, but the study does not define an independent animal activity curve or direct plant-partner temporal-matching exposure required by strict H1.
Multi-species understory study links flowering phenology, pollination and fruit/seed set across years, but phenological group/season is the exposure rather than a matched plant-partner timing metric.
Ozone treatment changes plant phenology, attractiveness to several pollinators and reproductive success through multiple pathways; no isolated plant-partner temporal-matching effect is identified.

Plant reproduction and mutualistic/antagonistic insect interactions vary across seasonal agroecological resource gradients, but the focal predictors are management/resource heterogeneity and interaction levels rather than a direct partner-matching exposure.

Urbanization affects flowering phenology and reproductive success while pollinator visitation/pollen deposition are measured, but the study does not estimate a direct flowering-partner synchrony effect on final reproduction.
Pollinator-exclusion evidence identifies wind as the primary pollen vector in Chamaedorea radicalis; no focal animal mutualist timing exposure for IWE.
Chamaedorea alternans is experimentally supported as wind-pollinated; thrips are observed but insect exclusion does not reduce seed production, so there is no focal animal mutualist timing effect.
Simulation study displacing Corydalis and Bombus phenologies; plant endpoint is simulated fraction of flowers pollinated rather than an observed final reproductive-fitness effect.
Banksia flowering phenology, bird visitation and seed set are described across species, but no direct plant-population matching exposure to a bird activity window is estimated.
Cypripedium flowering longevity, rare Bombus visitation and site fruit set are measured, but pollinator activity is not represented as a quantitative temporal matching exposure linked to fruit set.
Comparative orchid study relates flowering phenology/floral display to reproductive success and insect dependence, but lacks an independently measured pollinator activity window for strict matching.
Tibouchina study measures bee-guild activity periods and reproduction among co-flowering species, but does not estimate plant-partner temporal matching as the exposure for final plant fitness.
Duplicate bibliographic representation of the same Tibouchina pollinator-guild article screened under DOI 10.1590/S0085-56262011005000040; not an independent study.
Spatially explicit theoretical model of mast-seeding and specialist seed-predator dynamics; not a primary empirical timing-to-plant-fitness study.

Field experiments show mammalian herbivory reduces lifetime plant fitness and delayed phenology predicts herbivory susceptibility across a range boundary, but there is no within-season animal activity window or direct temporal matching metric.

Natural-history occurrence records and species-distribution/secondary-extinction models quantify plant-bee phenological mismatch, but the response is modeled extinction risk rather than observed final plant reproductive performance; proxy evidence only.

Experimental warming measures plant-pollinator temporal synchrony and both plant/bee fitness, but synchrony remains maintained while fitness declines through physiological/behavioral pathways; no recoverable mismatch-to-plant-fitness effect for strict H1.

Ficus altissima crop phenology and seed/pollinator reproductive success vary seasonally, but seasonal fitness variation is not estimated as a direct host-pollinator temporal-matching effect and is strongly linked to non-pollinating fig wasps.
Crop flowering and squash-bee emergence synchrony is quantified directly, but the study does not measure crop fruit/seed yield as a response to synchrony; plant final-fitness endpoint is absent.
Silene study quantifies fitness contributions of diurnal pollinators and Hadena, but the focal contrast is pollinator identity/service rather than plant-partner phenological matching.
